newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ferry owners fear end of duty free sales in 1999.
newsitem.headline: EU ferry owners fear end of duty free sales in 1999.

text.p: Scrapping duty- and tax-free sales in 1999 would destroy 50,000 jobs in the European Union, European shipowners predicted on Thursday but the European Commission said the move would go ahead as planned.
"The decision is taken. It is up to the industry to adapt. They were granted a long period for that," said Betty Olivi, the spokeswoman of EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti.

She was reacting to an industry study showing that the ending of duty free sales in the EU could lead to massive job losses in the ferry industry, sharply higher ticket prices and closures of routes in outlying regions.
The survey was published by the European Community Shipowners' Association (ECSA), the International Duty Free Confederation and the European Travel Research Foundation (ETRF).
"It is becoming increasingly clear that the abolition of duty and tax free sales will have major adverse implications for the maritime sector," said Alfons Guinier, ECSA secretary general.

The study, commissioned by the ETRF, forecast the loss of more than 50,000 jobs in ferry and tourism related sectors, the potential closures of routes in peripheral regions and average price rises on tickets of some 30 percent.
Nineteen routes would be lost in the British, Irish and German industries, ferry capacity would be halved in Finland and up to 30 ferry routes in northern Europe could close.
Fewer ferry routes and higher freight charges would also result in increased pollution and environmental damage.
"The proposed abolition of intra-EU duty and tax-free sales from June 1999 will significantly damage the EU ferry industry," the lobby groups said in a statement.
Guinier urged member states and the European Commission to review urgently the decision to close down the duty free industry, which had an EU turnover of $6.9 billion last year.
EU finance ministers decided in 1991 to scrap such sales, despite intense opposition from industry.

They agreed to a six-year extension to allow the sector time to adjust even though the purchase of goods without paying Value Added Tax or excise duties should have been abolished already in 1993 when the EU's single market was created.
To overturn that decision, finance ministers would need to agree unanimously.
But Olivi said it was unimaginable that they would reverse their decision given their budgetary constraints.

She also said the industry study had not taken into account jobs that would be gained by duty-paid retailers, adding that governments were in effect handing out subsidies to ferry companies by allowing duty-free sales.
Monti has made no secret of his belief that duty-free goods are incompatible with EU rules.

Britain's Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Company (P&O), Finnish-Swedish ferry group Silja Line and Sweden's Stena Line AB STENfb.ST were all present at the launch of the study on the impact of the abolition of duty free sales, warning about the serious consequences for their industry.
They said duty-frees had helped build up the maritime sector which was especially important for countries like Britain, Ireland, Finland and Sweden -- all heavily dependent on sea transport.
